title: Off the expected course
core: All three say a thing has left the path it was supposed to follow, and all three are the formal, analytic way to say it rather than the casual *weird* or *odd*. The difference is what supplies the path — a shared starting point, a predictive model, or a norm of proper functioning — and how much blame attaches to leaving it. They run from pure geometry to pure diagnosis: measuring an angle, flagging a misfit, reporting a failure.

words.nuance: The only one requiring a **common origin** — things must have started together to diverge, and the gap widens with distance. It attaches to paths, opinions, series, and evolutionary lines, never to a single freak reading. No standard is being violated; there is no "correct" branch.

Judged against a **model or prediction**, not an origin and not a norm of health. It says only *the data point does not fit* — deliberately withholding whether that means instrument error, noise, or a Nobel. A scientist reaches for it precisely because it commits to nothing.

The one that **assigns fault**. It measures against a proper course and reports failure, so it collocates with cells, behaviour, and conduct — things that can go wrong, not merely differ. Calling a reading aberrant already implies someone should explain and fix it.

exam_note: Sentence-equivalence traps swap **anomalous** for **aberrant**: check whether the sentence merely flags a misfit or already condemns it — and reject **divergent** wherever no shared starting point exists.
